human_tolerance.notes: It lives in open grassland and prairie and does not come into a garden, though it will dig burrows and eat vegetables in one that borders a lawn.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: It puts on a heavy layer of fat and stores food in its burrow in late summer, enters the nest in October, and rolls into a stiff ball; respiration falls from 100-200 breaths per minute to one breath about every five minutes. It emerges in March or early April, surviving over six months without food or water.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: The active season above ground. The article gives no calendar window for breeding, so this one is a judgement placed after the March or early-April emergence.

vocalizations.description: A bird-like trill, given after the squirrel has dived into its burrow and poked its nose back out. The trill is an alarm call and is most often used by females to warn nearby relatives.

taxonomy.note: Both databases place the species in Ictidomys, following the split of the paraphyletic genus Spermophilus by Helgen and colleagues that the article describes.

external.note: GBIF usage key and ITIS TSN read directly from the two databases; the iNaturalist taxon id via Wikidata (P3151).

common_names.note: Wikidata label 'thirteen-lined ground squirrel'; the article adds striped gopher, leopard ground squirrel and squinny as alternatives.

range.note: The article says only 'widely distributed over grasslands and prairies of North America' and gives no country list. Canada, the United States and Mexico are recorded because GBIF and Wikidata both list the species in all three; no finer claim is made here.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: It digs and occupies a 15-20 foot burrow with several side passages, walks and trots over the ground when foraging, and 'has a maximum running speed of 8 mph (13 km/h) and reverses direction if chased', which is why gallop is listed as a mode for the escape.

traits.thermoregulation.note: 'This species of hibernating ground squirrel' whose 'body temperature drops to 5-7 C' in torpor and returns to 37 C in arousal.

traits.flight.note: A ground squirrel with no wings and no gliding structure; 'None' follows from the description.

traits.nest_type.note: 'The burrow may be 15 to 20 feet long, with several side passages', most of it within one to two feet of the surface, with the hibernation nest in a deeper section and shorter burrows dug as hiding places.

traits.perching.note: False: the animal spends its time on the ground and in its burrow, and the quadruped body plan has no perched pose.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg 0.21 (< 1 kg). The size class depends on the estimated mass, which is itself derived; see traits.mass_kg.

traits.mass_kg.note: The article gives no mass for this species. 0.21 kg is the midpoint of 'at emergence from hibernation the squirrels weigh between 200 and 275 g for females' reported for Richardson's ground squirrel (Urocitellus richardsoni), the closest-sized close relative in the same subfamily. It is an estimate for a relative, not a measured value for I. tridecemlineatus.

traits.length_m.note: The article gives no length for this species. 0.2 m is a low-precision estimate of head-and-body length for a ground squirrel of the estimated mass above, and is approximate; it is not a sourced measurement for I. tridecemlineatus.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: Judgement: no open source gives a standing shoulder height for this species. Taken as about a third of the low-precision 0.2 m length above, which suits the species' low, flat-running ground-squirrel build; it is an estimate, not a sourced measurement.

traits.lifespan_y.note: The article describes six months of hibernation with almost complete metabolic suppression but gives no lifespan figure. 4.0 years is a deliberate low-precision estimate for a small ground squirrel with that hibernation pattern, and is approximate rather than sourced.

traits.diet.note: 'Its primary diet includes grass and weed seeds, caterpillars, grasshoppers, and crickets, but it may also eat mice and shrews; it will viciously attack and consume cicadas if able to catch them.' Shares are a judgement.

traits.social.note: 'A solitary or only somewhat colonial hibernator, it often occurs in aggregations in suitable habitats', with 'solitary habits, shown by agonistic behaviors to squirrels invading their own areas' and tail-flicking used to hold personal space; the group size is the size of a burrow aggregation.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'The thirteen-lined ground squirrel is strictly diurnal and is especially active on warm days.'

traits.defense.note: 'It is well known for standing upright to survey its domain, diving down into its burrow when it senses danger, then sometimes poking out its nose and giving a bird-like trill.'

traits.wariness.note: It dives at the slightest sense of danger, keeps agonistic distances from other squirrels, and checks the air by standing upright before feeding; a high wariness follows directly.

habitat.use.note: 'widely distributed over grasslands and prairies of North America', living in a burrow and foraging over open ground; all its time is terrestrial.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'diving down into its burrow when it senses danger' and overwintering in a deeper nest section of it; 'burrow' is the matching drawable shelter tag.

habitat.resources.note: Seed- and insect-dominated diet on open grassland with a burrow for shelter and escape; weights are judgement.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'This squirrel sometimes damages gardens by digging burrows and eating vegetables', which is tolerance of the reverse kind: the animal comes to a garden and acts on it rather than living in it. The habitat enum has no matching value for a species that treats a garden as a food opportunity rather than a habitat, so the least-wrong value is recorded and explained here.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'This species of hibernating ground squirrel'; 'It enters its nest in October... It emerges in March or early April', and it 'can survive in hibernation for over six months without food or water'.

seasonal.phases.note: The October entry and March or early-April emergence are stated; it also notes some adults retire much earlier. The breeding window is a judgement, since the article gives no calendar for breeding.

seasonal.life_stages.note: The article gives no gestation, litter size or juvenile period for this species. 45 days and a 0.6 scale are a deliberate low-precision estimate for a small sciurid and are approximate, not sourced.

seasonal.triggers.note: The article dates the cycle only by month - it enters its nest in October and emerges in March or early April - and notes the animal is 'especially active on warm days', but gives no temperature threshold. Entering below 0 C and leaving above 5 C is a judgement chosen to reproduce that October-to-March window on the northern Great Plains; it is not a sourced figure.

vocalizations.trill.note: 'diving down into its burrow when it senses danger, then sometimes poking out its nose and giving a bird-like trill. The "trill" is an alarm call that is most often used by females to warn nearby relatives.'

look.note: 'It is brownish, with 13 alternating brown and whitish longitudinal lines (sometimes partially broken into spots) on its back and sides, creating rows of whitish spots within dark lines'; the pale stripe colour is carried in the accent slot and the proportions and box placement are judgement.

behavior.note: The shared fsm-ground-forager-v1 program fits a ground-foraging herbivore that eats from the landscape, drinks and bolts for its burrow; food_tag is set to seed because seeds dominate the diet. rest_sun_lo_deg and rest_sun_hi_deg are set to -90 and -6 because the species is strictly diurnal, and flee_gait is set to gallop to match its documented 13 km/h escape run.
